summary: Commodity Futures Trading Commission head Brooksley Born called for greater disclosure and new rules for financial derivatives, but her recommendations were ignored.
News broke that two Bear Stearns hedge funds speculating in mortgage-backed securities were melting down, marking the start of the financial crisis.
Chris Dodd played a crucial role in crafting the controversial $700 billion Wall Street bailout package known as TARP during the financial crisis.
The Federal Reserve invoked emergency powers to lend money to Wall Street during the financial crisis, using authority from 1991 legislation.
Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy protection after other financial firms demand cash to protect their positions.
The federal government took over Freddie Mac, prompting the Freddie Mac Foundation to put all charitable grants on hold, including a $250,000 grant expected by a preschool serving needy children.

The US government rescues four major financial institutions—Bear Stearns, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Lehman Brothers—marking an unprecedented intrusion into the financial system and shaking faith in free markets.

The U.S. financial system faced its gravest crisis in modern times as Merrill Lynch and Lehman Brothers appeared almost certain to disappear and AIG sought a financial lifeline, one week after the government took over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson refused to extend taxpayer-backed loans to Lehman Brothers, causing prospective buyers to walk away and forcing the firm to declare bankruptcy, ending the "too entangled to fail" doctrine.
The article discusses the financial economic crisis, attributing it to moral failures and greed, and identifies speculators, short sellers, and foreclosures as three major causes.

Treasury Secretary Henry M. Paulson Jr., Federal Reserve Chairman Ben S. Bernanke, and New York Fed President Timothy F. Geithner have formed a close partnership to engineer the government's response to the gravest financial crisis in generations, making key decisions from the Bear Stearns rescue to the takeovers of Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and AIG.
The Federal Reserve provides an $85 billion loan to American International Group (AIG) as part of the financial crisis response.

The Federal Reserve, after pumping $100 billion into the banking system and lending $115 billion to rescue Bear Stearns and AIG, was forced to ask the Treasury to borrow extra money to replenish its coffers amid a severe financial crisis.
The collapse of Wall Street's business model, marked by Lehman Brothers' bankruptcy, Merrill Lynch's sale to Bank of America, and AIG's floundering, triggers a global financial crisis.
George Bush declares a pivotal moment for America's economy and calls for urgent government action, including federal purchase of illiquid mortgage assets, to address the financial crisis.
Barack Obama expresses support for Treasury and Federal Reserve efforts to address the financial crisis and outlines principles for an emergency response plan.
The Bush administration proposes a historic $500 billion bailout of financial firms to address the economic crisis.

The U.S. government has already put enormous taxpayer resources at risk by bailing out Bear Stearns, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and AIG, and proposing to buy risky assets from the banking system to stop the economy from plummeting into another depression.
New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg states that nobody knows what any institution owns, the terms of the securities they own, or what they are worth amid the financial crisis.
John McCain, under pressure from the financial crisis, called for the removal of SEC Chairman Chris Cox, a move criticized as unpresidential and fact-free.
President Bush warns that the credit crisis could devastate the U.S. economy unless Congress quickly approves a $700 billion bailout plan for the financial system.
The director of the Congressional Budget Office testifies that the proposed Wall Street bailout could worsen the financial crisis and even trigger additional failures of large institutions.
A columnist argues that the financial crisis stems from the financial sector's unsound practices of trading money backed by assets they never owned and that often lacked real value.
The financial crisis is described as the bankruptcy of modern economics, with financial markets verging on hysteria and threatening to drive the real economy into a deep recession or worse.
The Justice Department and SEC widen investigations into Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac amid the broader financial crisis, with the FBI also investigating 26 companies including AIG and Lehman Brothers.
Citigroup agrees to acquire Wachovia’s banking business in a government-urged rescue, with the FDIC limiting Citigroup’s losses on a $312 billion portfolio of troubled Wachovia loans.
House Republicans declined to support the administration's bailout plan amid the financial crisis, leading to a crisis of faith within the party.
A bipartisan rebellion in the House killed a $700 billion rescue plan for the nation's financial system, sending global stock prices plunging and dealing President Bush his worst legislative defeat.
The House of Representatives fails to pass an economic recovery package, prompting overwhelming public concern that the failure could deepen the financial crisis.

The Treasury Department issued a five-sentence notice changing tax policy to give U.S. banks a windfall of as much as $140 billion amid the financial crisis, drawing criticism that it exceeded legal authority.

Brooksley Born, head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, sought to regulate the fast-growing derivatives market, but was opposed by Alan Greenspan, Robert Rubin, and Arthur Levitt, who argued her agency lacked authority and that regulation would create uncertainty.
Brazil's automobile sales fell 11 percent from September to October, the industry's first monthly decline in five years, as credit dried up amid the global financial crisis.

Advice offered to solve the financial crisis is based on the wrong diagnosis and wrong remedy, with the problem originating from government policies and political directives that caused market signals to malfunction.

Hedge funds face investor withdrawals and are blamed by some analysts for propagating the high-risk culture that led to the Wall Street crisis, though analysts say it is hard to determine their exact blame due to secrecy.
U.S. factory orders fell 4 percent in August and new unemployment claims rose to a seven-year high of 497,000, signs that the economy was sliding toward recession amid the financial crisis.
The financial turmoil has pushed the Obama campaign into the lead, with the article attributing the crisis's roots to the Fed's flawed response to China rather than deregulation.
Global markets plunged and the World Bank president said the financial system may have reached a "tipping point," as the crisis continued despite passage of a $700 billion U.S. rescue package.

During a presidential debate, John McCain and Barack Obama clashed over the causes of the financial crisis, with McCain charging that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac "lit this fire" and Obama blaming McCain's pursuit of deregulation.
The stock market's prolonged tumble has wiped out about $2 trillion in Americans' retirement savings over the past 15 months, according to Congress's top budget analyst.

The financial crisis has gone global, with stock indexes falling and credit markets seizing up around the world, prompting calls for an internationally coordinated response at the upcoming IMF meeting.

The leaders of France, Germany, Italy, Britain and the European Commission met in Paris to discuss the worldwide economic crisis and issued a statement on ensuring the safety and stability of the worldwide banking system.

Concerns that tightening credit and an overall economic downturn will lead fewer people to buy new cars sent General Motors' stock price plunging 31 percent to close at $4.76, its lowest since 1950, while Ford Motor fell 21 percent to close at $2.08.
The worst financial crisis since the Great Depression is claiming another casualty: American-style capitalism, as the Bush administration considers a partial nationalization of some banks.

The global financial crisis exposes the vulnerability of America's retirement system, as steep stock market declines erode 401(k) savings and prompt questions about relying on the stock market for retirement.

Governments around the world took unprecedented steps to rescue the global financial system, with major European powers unveiling a united plan to prevent further bank failures while Australia and New Zealand moved to calm panicked investors by guaranteeing deposits before stock markets opened in Asia.

The U.S. government plans to invest $250 billion in the country's banks, forcing nine of the largest to accept a Treasury stake in what amounts to a partial nationalization, as part of its escalating response to the financial crisis.

The US government, led by Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson, moved aggressively to stabilize the financial system by flooding banks with dollars, expanding deposit insurance, guaranteeing new bank debt, and injecting capital into healthy banks, resulting in the biggest one-day stock market rally in 70 years.
Swiss investors withdraw funds from UBS amid concerns about the global credit crisis, as the bank has written off $43 billion in loser investments since 2007.
President Bush announced plans to host an emergency summit of leaders from the world's top economies to map out a response to the global financial crisis.
European leaders press for a new Bretton Woods-style summit to address the global financial crisis, with French President Nicolas Sarkozy securing President Bush's agreement to hold it.
Critics argue that mark-to-market accounting rules worsen the financial crisis, while others contend the meltdown stems from excessive bad financial bets with borrowed money.
Chinese local officials made emergency bailout payments to workers after Chong Yik Toy Co. went bankrupt amid the global financial crisis.

Alan Greenspan, former Federal Reserve chairman, acknowledged before a congressional committee that his long-held free-market ideology was flawed and that certain financial derivatives should be regulated, as the global financial crisis devastated world markets.

Employers are aggressively cutting jobs and reducing costs in response to the nation's economic crisis, with mass layoffs in September reaching their highest level since September 2001 and nearly half a million Americans filing new unemployment claims in each of the past four weeks.

Oil-exporting nations are forced to spend billions to prop up their domestic banks, currencies, and stock markets as tumbling crude prices compound the global financial crisis, ahead of an OPEC emergency meeting expected to cut output.
The global financial crisis worsens the food crisis, with Oxfam estimating that economic turmoil this year has pushed an additional 119 million people below the poverty line.

Barack Obama's election victory is attributed in large measure to the financial crisis and the prospect of the longest and deepest economic downturn in a quarter-century, with his presidency facing the task of beginning recovery.
President Bush declares the global economic crisis a decisive moment for the global economy as leaders of the 20 largest economies head to Washington for an emergency meeting.
Leaders of the Group of 20 countries meet to build on an international strategy for responding to the financial crisis and to address the sharp downturn in the world economy.

Treasury Secretary Henry M. Paulson Jr., reversing his long-held opposition, is urging regulation of hedge funds and plans to propose broad new federal authority to take over any failing financial institution amid the worst financial crisis in nearly a century.
President-elect Barack Obama selects New York Federal Reserve Bank President Timothy F. Geithner as Treasury secretary to lead the response to the financial crisis.

Citigroup's stock price fell 60 percent over one week amid investor concerns about the bank's ability to weather the economic crisis, as executives launched a campaign to convince investors and analysts of the company's strong position.

The chiefs of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund declined to participate in a major UN conference on financing for development assistance for poor countries, amid the global financial crisis.

The Federal Reserve is lending $893 billion to a wide range of institutions to help them weather the economic storm, far exceeding the Treasury Department's $250 billion financial rescue program, largely outside public view.
China declines to take a global leadership role amid the financial crisis, arguing it can do the most good by focusing on its own domestic economic and political problems.
France announced a $33 billion economic stimulus plan to counter the economic fallout from the financial crisis, while the European Central Bank and Bank of England cut interest rates.
Peruvian President Alan García announces a $3.4 billion bailout package to help the national economy amid the global financial crisis.

President-elect Barack Obama announces key financial regulatory appointments, including Daniel Tarullo to the Federal Reserve Board, Mary Schapiro to head the SEC, and Gary Gensler to chair the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, stating that overhauling financial regulation will be a top priority amid the ongoing financial crisis.

President George W. Bush announced federal financial assistance to troubled U.S. automakers, citing the global financial crisis and recession as reasons to intervene rather than allow a disorderly bankruptcy.

Policymakers are considering restructuring Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, including possibly eliminating them, after their collapse amid the U.S. housing and mortgage crisis led to a government takeover in September.
One month after world leaders vowed at a Washington summit to combat the global financial crisis collectively and adhere to free-market principles, a number of nations are putting up roadblocks.

Governors from several U.S. states call for a bold $1 trillion federal economic recovery package to address the ongoing financial crisis, emphasizing infrastructure, safety-net programs, housing, education, and middle-class tax cuts.

SEC Chairman Christopher Cox defends his restrained approach to the financial crisis, saying he provided steady leadership and was not responsible for the agency's failure to detect the alleged $50 billion Madoff fraud.
Paul Volcker was appointed chairman of President Obama's Economic Recovery Advisory Board, bringing credibility to Obama's campaign amid the worst economic crisis since the Great Depression.
GMAC relinquished its exclusive right to provide financing to people buying General Motors vehicles in exchange for up to $6 billion in federal aid, ending a 10-year contract between GM and GMAC.

The U.S. government's escalating borrowing amid the financial crisis raises concerns about its ability to repay, with markets pricing a 6 percent probability of U.S. default over the next 10 years, up from 1 percent a year earlier.

The global economic crisis is argued to potentially benefit democracy by weakening nondemocratic "authoritarian capitalist" regimes such as China, Russia, Venezuela, and Iran, though some democracies may also be at risk.

A top economic adviser to the incoming Obama administration unveils a plan to radically rethink the global financial system, including measures that would dramatically expand government control over banking and investment in the United States.

U.S. government officials are considering a "bad bank" plan to quarantine troubled assets as part of efforts to address the ongoing financial crisis, amid concerns that more than the remaining $320 billion in rescue funds may be needed.
Tim Geithner brands China a currency manipulator at his confirmation hearings, signaling a possible shift in US-China relations amid debate over China's role in the financial crisis.

Companies across America are rapidly reshaping themselves in response to the spreading financial crisis, with Pfizer announcing a $68 billion acquisition of Wyeth and 8,000 job cuts, Intel closing its last Silicon Valley plant and cutting over 5,000 jobs, and Home Depot closing its 34-store Expo chain.
Timothy Geithner is confirmed by the Senate as Treasury secretary, taking charge of the U.S. response to the financial crisis and the deepest recession in at least a generation.

The article analyzes three distinct but interwoven crises—collapsing consumer spending, the financial crisis, and a global trade crisis—facing President Obama, and questions whether the proposed economic stimulus plan can produce a lasting recovery.

A congressional panel overseeing the government's financial bailout concludes that the economic crisis could have been prevented with better regulation and calls for a raft of proposals to overhaul government oversight of the financial sector.
President Obama acknowledged he would be a one-term president if the economic stimulus does not work, as the Senate opened debate on a nearly $900 billion stimulus plan.

The Federal Reserve has used unconventional, aggressive programs during the financial crisis to make hundreds of billions of dollars available for mortgages, auto and credit card lending, and businesses, fueling fierce debate over its expanded market role.

President Obama declares in his first prime-time news conference that saving and creating jobs is more important than bipartisan cooperation and presses for a massive economic stimulus plan, warning that inaction could turn the crisis into a catastrophe.
Treasury Secretary Tim Geithner outlines a new financial stability plan to restart credit flow, strengthen banks, and aid homeowners and small businesses amid the economic crisis.
Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner unveils a bank-bailout plan whose lack of detail dismayed lawmakers and investors and triggered a steep sell-off on Wall Street.

Justice Department and FBI officials commit to investigating more than 530 cases of alleged corporate malfeasance, including 38 investigations of name-brand businesses and financial institutions involved in the financial crisis.

The Office of Thrift Supervision calls for mortgage lenders to halt foreclosures until the Obama administration implements a program to help struggling homeowners, amid the financial and economic crisis.
Congress approved a $787 billion stimulus package aimed at creating jobs and reviving the economy amid the worst economic downturn in a generation.

President Obama unveiled a foreclosure-prevention package pouring more than $75 billion into helping as many as 9 million homeowners obtain more affordable mortgage terms as part of efforts to address the nation's economic crisis.
SEC Chairman Mary Schapiro plans to examine whether the boards of banks and other financial firms conducted effective oversight leading up to the financial crisis.

The global financial crisis strains US-China trade relations, with Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner accusing China of currency manipulation and China criticizing the "Buy America" program as "poison to the solution" of the crisis.

President Obama addressed a joint session of Congress, outlining his plans for economic recovery and promising to lead an economic renewal to lift the country out of its crisis without bankrupting its future.
President Obama's budget proposal projects a $1.75 trillion deficit, 12.3 percent of GDP, for the current fiscal year amid the dire economic climate.
Royal Bank of Scotland reports the largest annual corporate loss in British history of 24.14 billion pounds for 2008 and confirms it will offload toxic assets into a government insurance program.

The Obama administration engineers bailout initiatives so firms can avoid congressional restrictions, including executive pay limits, by channeling funds through special entities rather than providing direct aid.
A discussion questions whether those who managed their finances responsibly have a moral obligation to bail out those who did not amid the financial crisis.

An article argues that President Obama's agenda to transform health care, education, and energy is not the cause of or cure for the financial crisis, and that he had yet to unveil a plan to deal with the banking crisis.

The World Bank warns that the global economy will shrink in 2009 for the first time since the 1940s, as the financial crisis that began in the United States drags developing nations into the first global recession since World War II.
Federal Reserve Chairman Ben S. Bernanke called the financial crisis the worst since the 1930s and advocated overhauling financial regulation and revising mark-to-market accounting rules.
Jon Stewart criticizes CNBC and Jim Cramer for failing to warn the public about the risky Wall Street conduct that triggered the financial crisis.

France and Germany appealed to fellow European nations to take the lead in emphasizing tighter regulation and a new global financial architecture to combat the world economic crisis and prevent new ones.

Chinese companies have been on a global shopping spree, snapping up tens of billions of dollars' worth of key assets in Iran, Brazil, Russia, Venezuela, Australia and France in a fire sale set off by the financial crisis.
Federal Reserve officials knew for months about bonuses at AIG but failed to tell the Obama administration, exposing problems in a relationship vital to addressing the financial crisis.

Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben S. Bernanke pressed Congress to grant the federal government unprecedented new power to seize non-bank financial firms whose collapse could jeopardize the world financial system.
The International Monetary Fund rolled out reforms, including a new flexible credit line and doubled lending limits, aimed at making it more effective in combating the global economic crisis.
EU President and Czech Prime Minister Mirek Topolanek criticizes the Obama administration's economic policies, calling its deficit spending and bank bailouts "a road to hell."
The United States is warned to be resembling emerging markets like Argentina and Russia in the causes of and responses to its ongoing economic and financial crisis.

World leaders at the London summit are set to give major developing countries including China, India, and Brazil unprecedented new influence in global financial decisions in response to the financial crisis.
China signed $138 million in loan packages with Jamaica in March, becoming Jamaica's biggest financial partner amid the global financial crisis.
World leaders at the G-20 meeting in London pledged to quadruple the IMF's resources and strengthen its mandate in response to the global economic crisis.

Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, facing scrutiny over his tenure as New York Fed president, leads the push for the biggest expansion of financial regulation since the Great Depression and joins President Obama at the G20 meeting in London to discuss global financial regulatory reform.

Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke has amassed great influence in fighting the global economic crisis by committing trillions of dollars to keep markets afloat, radically redefining the Fed and risking serious inflation.
The global financial crisis threatens to undo more than a decade of economic and democratic progress in Africa by reducing investment, exports and aid.
Financial planners offer new investing principles for the post-crisis era after the stock market plunge revealed that many investors' risk tolerance was lower than they thought.
President Obama plans to attend the Summit of the Americas in Trinidad and Tobago, where Latin American leaders are expected to criticize the United States' role in the global financial crisis.

An opinion piece criticizes Larry Summers as a central, often overlooked cause of the global financial crisis, arguing his inflated reputation as a "Brain Bubble" shielded him from scrutiny and led to repeated policy errors such as failing to regulate derivatives.
The article compares the 2009 financial crisis to the Great Depression, noting that governments have eased credit and increased spending to arrest an economic free fall, unlike during the Depression.
David Kellermann, acting chief financial officer of Freddie Mac, was found dead in an apparent suicide at his Fairfax County home after months of intense stress related to the financial crisis.

Richard A. Posner publishes 'A Failure of Capitalism,' a book analyzing the causes of the financial crisis, arguing that the main villains are Alan Greenspan and George W. Bush rather than greed or stupidity.

Ontario towns with a collective population of nearly 500,000 retaliated against US "Buy American" provisions by effectively barring US companies from their municipal contracts, in what is described as the first shot in a larger campaign amid the global economic crisis.

Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner's implementation of key financial crisis policies has bogged down due to unfilled top positions, ad-hoc management, and unresolved decisions, delaying initiatives such as the toxic-asset relief program.

The Obama administration is actively discussing the creation of a regulatory commission with broad authority to protect consumers of financial products, as one of its first proposals to address causes of the financial crisis such as predatory mortgage lending.

Analysts explain that the financial crisis spread because the repo market, where banks borrowed short-term cash against collateral, collapsed when subprime losses caused depositors to demand larger haircuts and a flight to quality.

BankUnited collapsed as the largest bank failure so far this year, with the FDIC expecting to absorb $4.9 billion in losses, amid a federal investigation revealing that its regulator allowed the bank to cover up its financial weakness.

France's extensive social programs and government spending have shielded many citizens, such as retirees and public-sector workers, from the worst effects of the global economic crisis, though the country still faces rising unemployment and economic contraction.

Brooksley Born, former head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is reported to have accurately predicted over a decade earlier that over-the-counter derivatives could play a crucial role in a financial crisis like the one that convulsed America, though her efforts to regulate them were blocked by influential Washington figures.

Senior administration officials are considering creating a single agency to regulate the banking industry as part of a sweeping overhaul of financial regulation aimed at preventing future financial crises.

Commentators debate whether Bill Clinton's failure to regulate derivatives contributed to the financial crisis, while noting the derivatives market grew 300 percent between 2003 and 2008 after he left office.

Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke, reflecting on the financial crisis, described it as resembling a classic 19th-century bank panic and defended the Fed's innovative measures to restore liquidity.

Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke warns that large sustained budget deficits could deepen the financial crisis and choke off the economy, urging Congress and the administration to commit to long-term fiscal sustainability.

The Obama administration names Kenneth R. Feinberg as a "compensation czar" with power to determine pay, including retirement packages, for senior executives at seven firms that received large federal bailouts amid the financial crisis.
The administration will put forward a plan to modernize financial regulation and supervision in response to the most severe financial crisis since the Great Depression.

BlackRock agrees to acquire Barclays Global Investors, creating the world's largest money manager with $2.7 trillion in assets, as its CEO defends the firm's stability amid concerns about systemic risk following the financial crisis.
The Obama administration proposes to abolish the Office of Thrift Supervision and roll its responsibilities into a new national banking regulatory agency.
President Obama is expected to unveil a plan to overhaul the financial regulatory system in response to the economic crisis.

A survey finds that hedge fund managers and executives view "onerous government regulation" as the biggest threat to their industry amid the financial crisis, with 38 percent citing it as the top concern.

The financial crisis that started in the United States is intensifying debate over whether the dollar should remain the world's dominant currency, with Brazil, Russia, India and China jointly declaring the need for a more diversified international monetary system.

General Electric became the largest beneficiary of the Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program after regulators loosened eligibility requirements, allowing its financing arm GE Capital to issue nearly a quarter of the $340 billion in government-backed debt.
